This Transit Camper Van Has a Handcrafted Interior With Home-Like Comforts Hidden in Plain Sight
14 photos
Photo: YouTube Screenshot / LiamTheTerrible
There are endless ways in which you can customize a camper van. Some people prefer all-out luxurious builds that try to come as close to a conventional home, while others, like me, look for relatively simpler builds. The conversion I'd like to share with you today is part of the latter category.
What we have here is a build based on a 2022 Ford Transit with a high roof. It was created by Coalition Vans, a Sheffield, UK-based company specializing in custom camper van conversions. We've covered some of its projects here on autoevolution, such as a bespoke Transit-based mobile home .
On the outside, this Transit has few upgrades. The most significant ones are four tinted, double-glazed windows: two at the rear and two on the sides. By the way, since the vehicle is a right-hand-drive, the driver's side is the one on the right.
Other notable mods are an electric hookup point and rails on the roof that hold a 450 W solar array. These are quite subtle, so for most people, this van could pass as a standard van and not a camper.
Inside is where you'll find the biggest transformation. Instead of an empty cargo van interior, you'll be greeted by a bright, well-organized interior. It has a closed layout, with the driver's cabin mostly separated from the living space.
Photo: YouTube Screenshot / LiamTheTerrible I said "mostly separated" because there's no wall like you'd find in most vans with closed layouts. Instead, the kitchen is the dividing part, but it leaves a bit of space to let some light shine through.
You could even jump from one area to the other if needed in an emergency. What's more, if you want privacy or to block the light coming from the cabin, you can use a roll-down curtain to separate the two areas. Above it, there's a spacious headliner shelf offering storage space.
Regarding aesthetics, the customer opted for wood-imitating vinyl plank flooring, white laminated cabinetry, and a white clad ceiling. The look is complemented by a butcher block countertop, teal couch cushion upholstery, and a blue tiled backsplash.
The kitchen features a black fridge with a tiny freezer compartment, a single-burner induction stovetop with a hinged top, and a pop-up socket that offers standard plugs and USB outlets. What's more, a Maxxair vent fan above is perfectly positioned to draw out the smells and fumes from cooking.
Photo: YouTube Screenshot / LiamTheTerrible An overhead shelf with a bungee cord, a drawer, a cabinet underneath the stove, and a cupboard are available for storage. What's more, there are two units by the entrance, each with a top and three shelves – the best part about them is that they're curved so you don't hurt yourself if you bump into them.
Next, we have a floor-to-ceiling unit on the passenger side. It has a closet with a hanging rail, as well as a cupboard with three shelves.
The rear part of the living space seems relatively simple at first sight. It comprises two long benches with backrests, one on each side, and a Lagun table mount with a decently sized top.
Four or more people can sit comfortably here and enjoy a meal or play some board games. You'll also notice five overhead cabinets, a massive wall niche with two bungee cords, and a compartment closer to the kitchen that houses a portable toilet.
Photo: YouTube Screenshot / LiamTheTerrible There's more than meets the eye in this part of the van. First, the benches have hinged tops that can be lifted to reveal storage spaces. This is usually where you also find the utility systems – but not in this van.
Since there's no sink or shower in the rig, there's no plumbing system. As for power, Coalition Vans managed to fit the electrical system in the driver's cabin, below the passenger bench and behind the driver's seat. Its highlights are a 460 Ah battery bank and a 2,000 W inverter.
Three charging sources are available: solar power , shore power, and DC-DC charging while the engine is running. If used correctly and efficiently, you could technically never run out of power, especially since the van has just two big power consumers: the fridge and the stove.
The panel behind the driver-side bench is actually not a wall. Pull it down by using a small cut-out, and you'll discover that it's part of a Murphy bed system. The panel folds all the way down, revealing a mattress, charging points, and a wall niche that mirrors the one on the opposite side.
Photo: YouTube Screenshot / LiamTheTerrible All in all, this fresh conversion by Coalition Vans keeps things simpler but still manages to pack a surprising amount of comforts inside a compact interior.
What makes this project even more impressive than what we've already seen is that the whole interior was hand-built. Even though each van they make is different, Coalition Vans takes time to create each design by hand, not by using CNC machines like most converters.

By Alexander Whiteman
27 October 2026
Shippers are scrambling to make alternative arrangement for inland container movements in the UK after a train derailment forced the suspension of rail services to key terminals in the south-east, including DP World London Gateway.
More than 1km of track was torn up by storms that battered the region on Friday, with Forth Ports notifying customers that no rail services would be servicing Tilbury or Tilbury 2 this week.
A spokesperson for DP World told The Loadstar : “We are currently operating a reduced rail freight service from our London Gateway terminal. We are working closely with customers and with Network Rail to minimise disruption while repairs to the network are carried out.”
Hapag-Lloyd has warned customers that inland cargo movements were likely to be impacted, advising them to arrange road transport for any containers booked under merchant haulage arrangements.
For customers using carrier haulage, the German liner noted that its inland team would discuss alternative transport arrangements, but warned it would be unable to accept additional haulage requests during the disruption.
Whether there is sufficient trucking capacity to absorb the displaced rail volumes remains unclear, but as with much of the world, the UK’s haulage industry has been contending with a decades-long crisis in attracting new talent.
A spokesperson for the Road Haulage Association told The Loadstar it was “monitoring the situation and will support members however we can”, but was unable to give any detail on the expected level of demand provoked by two key gateways out of service for at least a week.
Hapag-Lloyd added it was monitoring the situation and would provide further updates as information became available, but the timetable for restoring normal rail freight operations, the number of containers affected, and the scale of any backlog all had yet to be established.

MIAMI BEACH — Miami International Airport has signed with Kalé Logistics Systems to set up the world’s first AI-based air cargo community system designed to streamline data exchange and communication between supply chain stakeholders on a centralized platform, with the goal of eliminating time-consuming paper-based transactions and manual scheduling that contributes to truck congestion.
Kalé offers cargo community systems and cargo management systems for ground handling companies at more than 125 airports and also runs single digital ecosystems at more than 75 maritime ports.
The air cargo community system combines various modules designed to simplify various tasks such as scheduling truck pick up and delivery at airport terminals, transmitting electronic delivery orders, electronic payments and filing customs documents. The idea is for airlines, logistics companies, motor carriers, customs brokers, warehouse operators and regulators to exchange data on a common platform that automatically routes the information to the correct party rather than relying on fragmented manual processes and systems, each with their own unique procedures.
Existing systems are credited with simplifying management of landside operations, providing granular insights into cargo flows, facilitating regulatory processes and improving end-to-end shipment visibility.
“This is about making Miami International Airport more future-ready: simplifying and expediting the movement of goods through our global gateway, supporting the businesses and jobs that depend on international trade, and ensuring that our airport remains an industry leader not just in cargo volume, but also in efficiency and sustainability,” said Miami-Dade County Mayor Daniella Levine Cava in a news release announcing the project.
The mayor also spoke about the benefits of the air cargo community system during a press conference on Tuesday at The International Air Cargo Association ’s biannual convention here.
Miami International Airport handled a record 3.4 million tons of freight in 2025, up 9.4% since 2024. It is has surpassed Chicago and Los Angeles as the busiest non-express cargo airport in the continental United States and the largest in the world for international capacity, excluding narrow-body aircraft.
MIA’s cargo traffic is made possible by about 190 cargo-only flights per day and more than 1,600 daily truck trips. Airport and country officials say that coordinating truck trips so that truckers don’t arrive unannounced and create long queues while they sort out paperwork and payments will significantly improve efficiency and carbon emissions.
Atlanta-based Kalé will hold community workshops starting in January to gather input about stakeholder requirements and expectations and then implement the system over a period of 18 months, CEO Amar More told FreightWaves.
Some airports only deploy a handful of modules, but MIA plans to implement the whole cargo community system, starting with electronic document sharing and truck traffic management, he said.
Kalé’s system will sit on the front end and have application programming interfaces, or middleware, that connect to each entity involved in moving cargo through MIA.
Why It Matters: Cargo trucks traditionally arrive at airports with limited information about the load and its availability for pickup, causing congestion at busy times. The new platform is expected to improve information sharing, advanced planning and truck scheduling, and help reduce waiting times at MIA. It will also allow MIA to connect with other airports for better planning of international imports and exports.
“Today, as a freight forwarder or a trucking company in Miami, you’re accessing one system at a time. A truck that goes and drops off at Worldwide Flight Services can’t easily coordinate its next move to pick up cargo at the Swissport ground handling facility,” More said in an interview.
Artificial intelligence will guide the parties through their workflows. Using traffic pattern prediction and wait time data, it will tell truckers, for example, how much time they can expect to spend unloading at their first destination and when to optimally schedule an appointment at the next ground handling facility for pick up, he explained. Truckers can query a generative chatbot in English or Spanish, to get information, such as whether a shipment is ready for pick up.
AI will also help terminal operators identify trade flows and patterns, perhaps alerting them in September to expect an influx of electronic shipments because a technology company is launching a new product.
In another AI use case, a documentation agent will allow users to upload a PDF copy of a document and it will convert the information into the format the receiver’s system can accept.
Kalé systems are currently operating at airports in Atlanta, Boston and at the Worldwide Flight Services facility at JFK New York, with implementation underway in Philadelphia and at Chicago-Rockford.
Some of the most established air cargo community systems are in Europe. Brussels airport was one of the first to implement such a system, powered by Nallian. It requires companies doing business at the airport to connect to its shared platform.
Participation in the United States, so far, is voluntary. More said the adoption rate is about 90% at the WFS facility in New York, with other locations at about 60% to 70% participation levels.
“The best community systems in the world have 98% to 99% adoption and that’s where the airport actually takes leadership and says, ‘Look, this is good for the overall community. If you have any concerns, let’s address those concerns. But, let’s get this done for everybody’. It’s a little bit of pain for 10 or 15 days, but then it falls in place,” More said.

Chattanooga–The Transportation Intermediaries Association (TIA) was quick out of the box earlier this year after two key court decisions that didn’t favor the brokerage community, asking the federal government for some sort of guidance for 3PLs: tell us what sort of carrier hiring practices would protect us.
Chris Burroughs is the head of TIA and he told an audience at the FreightWaves Broker Compliance Symposium here on Monday that what the TIA is seeking through its request for a federal rulemaking would take a long time to arrive, earlier efforts having stalled out.
“It’s no secret that carrier selection has been problematic for a very long time,” Burroughs said in an interview at the FreightWaves Broker Compliance Symposium here. (Full disclosure: the author of this article conducted the on-stage interview with Burroughs). “I’ve been at TIA for 15 years, and we were having these arguments when I first started that hey, we’ve got to figure out and provide more clarity and eliminate the confusion that exists in the carrier selection process.”
The issue is now more stark than ever. While Montgomery vs. Caribe stripped the brokerage community of the liability and negligence protection that had (mostly) been afforded under the Federal Aviation Administration Authorization Act (F4A), it became an even bigger issue not that many weeks later when C.H. Robinson was hit with a more than $600 million nuclear verdict– now at more than $700 million –as a result of a jury award involving a carrier hired by C.H. Robinson (NASDAQ: CHRW) that had a Satisfactory rating from the Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration (FMCSA).
The TIA’s request for a federal rulemaking on the issue occurred between the Montgomery decision and the nuclear verdict in the case of Lipe vs. Lupus Superior.
A long history of efforts
Burroughs recapped a long list of efforts on the legislative and regulatory side to get some sort of guidance on carrier selection that could be used as part of a courtroom defense. He described negotiations with the association of trial lawyers that would constantly get sidetracked by their opposition as being like Lucy pulling the football away from Charlie Brown.
The launch of Commercial, Safety, Accountability scores in 2010 was seen as a way to advance guidance on carrier selection, Burroughs said. “That was supposed to be the answer to tie a data-driven product to a safety rating,” Burroughs said. “Ultimately, that never happened.”
Chris Burroughs (l) and John Kingston at FreightWaves’ F3 Broker Compliance Symposium
Even the brokerage industry’s desire for changes softened somewhat when the industry began winning some cases through the protection of F4A, Burroughs said.
Behind the recent petition for a federal rulemaking, Burroughs said, is saying to FMCSA “hey, you are the federal agency that’s in charge of providing safety ratings to motor carriers. We want you to put forward a federal standard, taking it out of Congress’ hands because of the dysfunction and putting it back in the agency’s hands, where we believe it belongs.”
But he added, “rulemaking takes a long time.”
Guidance would be a help
A more short-term answer might be for FMCSA to issue guidance , Burroughs said. The guidance might say, according to Burroughs, “hey, these are the five or six things, whatever they come up, that should be checked prior to selecting a trucking company, and that would serve as kind of a pseudo carrier selection standard.”
FMCSA has a private document of high-risk carriers, Burroughs said. One of the requests TIA has made of the agency is to publish that list as well
The brokerage community is also the target of lawsuits filed by plaintiffs who are funded by venture capital companies. (It was discussed how Paul Clement, who represented Shawn Montgomery before the Supreme Court, is the “Michael Jordan” of attorneys who argue before the high court. Burroughs declined with a smile to estimate on what Clement was getting paid by the hour).
“They’re seeing blood in the water,” Burroughs said.
Tough choices to be made
The quandary that C.H. Robinson now faces in Lipe vs. Lupus Superior is that the ruling was not only expensive. It also involved a finding that the driver in the crash, who was killed, was essentially a C.H. Robinson employee. That sort of ruling, if it established a precedent, would open the door to even greater litigation hitting brokers.
But the clock is ticking at an annual rate of more than 6% interest on the now $700-million judgement which began at $603 million. A settlement would end the process but leave the finding about the driver’s relationship to C.H. Robinson intact.
Burroughs said C.H. Robinson’s strategy is clear: it is going to fight the verdict and not settle the case, which came out of a Dallas County courthouse.
“I’ve talked to (C.H. Robinson CEO) Dave Bozeman and (chief legal officer) Dorothy Capers,” Burroughs said. “They’re clearly going through the appeal process. They’re not going to settle the case.” He also expressed confidence based on those conversations that C.H. Robinson can win on appeal.
Better news on insurance
One of the potential negative impacts from the dual hits of Montgomery and Lipe was expected to be seen in insurance rates paid by brokers.
Burroughs said soon after the decision, “there was a two to four week period where rates were extremely high in terms of renewal.” Much of that was timing, he added; TIA members who renewed just before that period “hit the lottery.”
But that trend has calmed, according to Burroughts. “We’re not seeing any sort of massive, drastic increase in terms of insurance rates at double digits,” he said.

Waymo vs Tesla driverless miles per week, all markets (Credit: Robotaxi Tracker)
Elon Musk says Tesla’s Robotaxi race against Waymo “was never a real contest” after Tesla’s driverless fleet logged 438,000 miles in Austin in a single week, edging past Waymo’s 406,000 weekly average in the city.
That’s one city, one week, and a Waymo figure that’s four months old. Across the US, Waymo still drives about seven times more driverless miles than Tesla every week.
Where the chart comes from
The chart going around comes from Robotaxi Tracker , a community project that pulls driverless mileage from each company’s own reports: Tesla’s weekly Robotaxi safety report and Waymo’s quarterly Safety Impact data hub.
Jason Scharf posted the Austin view on X with the comment that “the battle for Autonomous Austin might already be over.” Musk replied overnight: “It was never a real contest.”
Advertisement - scroll for more content
The Austin data is real –albeit with some caveats. In the week ending October 18, Tesla reported 438,000 miles with no safety monitor aboard in Austin, up 30% from the week before. Waymo averaged about 406,000 miles a week in Austin in the second quarter.
But the tracker’s own caption explains the catch. Tesla’s figure is its latest week. Waymo’s is an average of April through June, because Waymo publishes about three months after each quarter ends. So Musk is comparing Tesla’s best week ever to Waymo’s spring.
The national picture isn’t close
Switch the same chart to “All markets” and the story flips.
Waymo averaged 3.90 million rider-only miles per week in Q2 2026. Tesla did 558,000 miles in its best week. Waymo’s Phoenix, Bay Area, and Los Angeles markets each drive more miles per week on their own than Tesla’s entire network.
Cumulative numbers are even more lopsided. Waymo has logged 271.3 million rider-only miles since 2020, including 50.7 million in Q2 alone, as we covered when Waymo released its latest safety data . Tesla has 3.11 million driverless miles since January 22, 2026. Waymo drove more than that in a single week.
And Tesla’s total leans almost entirely on one city:
Tesla Robotaxi market | Driverless miles, week to Oct 18
Austin | 438,000
Dallas | 94,841
Houston | 7,288
Tampa | 6,131
Orlando | 6,008
Miami | 5,626
Austin accounts for 79% of Tesla’s weekly driverless miles. Houston, Tampa, Orlando, and Miami combined did about 25,000 miles. Waymo’s smallest tracked market, Atlanta, averaged 250,000 a week in Q2.
Tesla flooded Austin with Cybercabs
The Austin surge has an obvious cause. Tesla launched public Cybercab rides in Austin on September 3.
According to Robotaxi Tracker’s count of the Texas DMV automated-vehicle list, Tesla now has 463 Cybercabs registered in Texas, 337 of them added in the last 30 days. That’s 48% of the 970 autonomous vehicles Tesla has registered in the state.
Tesla isn’t hiding the strategy. On the Q3 earnings call last week, Ashok Elluswamy, Tesla’s head of AI software, said the company wants to “swarm Austin with Cybercabs everywhere.” Musk said the Austin Cybercab fleet had grown “by a factor of 10” in about a month.
So Tesla dumped hundreds of new, company-owned cars into one metro and the miles went up. That’s fleet deployment. It doesn’t show the software can do what Waymo does in 15 cities, and Tesla can’t repeat it everywhere at once.
Still limited by safety, by Tesla’s own admission
The bigger problem is what the cars are allowed to do.
On the same earnings call, Elluswamy described the service as constrained by the software, not by regulators. He said that if there’s “the slightest possible risk at all,” Tesla doesn’t take it on, and that the limits are “technology driven” for now. Service hours only recently stretched from 9 p.m. toward 2 a.m., and he listed highways, “higher speed roads,” 24/7 operation, and more weather conditions as things Tesla still has to unlock.
You can see those limits in the rides. Tesla Robotaxis don’t take highways, and riders report they avoid at-grade railroad crossings. In September, a rider had a 10-minute Cybercab trip in Austin turn into a 70-minute detour because the car drove south through East Austin until it found a bridge over the rail line, instead of taking MoPac.
That matters for this comparison, too. Miles is a flattering metric when your car takes the long way. A trip that should cover a few miles and instead loops across town logs a lot more mileage for the same rider.
Waymo, meanwhile, has been taking riders on freeways in Phoenix, San Francisco, and Los Angeles since November 2025.
Electrek’s Take
Credit where it’s due: Tesla’s driverless miles are growing fast, 30% in a single week, and Austin now has a real Tesla fleet carrying the public without anyone in the driver’s seat. A year ago, that wasn’t the case.

What stands out to us is the type of autonomy Tesla is deploying. In 2020, Musk wrote that “Waymo is impressive, but a highly specialized solution,” and that Tesla’s approach was “a general solution.” For years, Tesla fans dismissed Waymo as a geofenced system that only worked in mapped areas with lots of restrictions.

The way courts decide who is responsible when a contracted truck ends up in a wreck is changing faster than most of the freight industry realizes, and the shift is not about one ruling or one eye-popping dollar figure, it is a whole direction of travel that keeps pulling responsibility up the chain toward brokers and the companies that arrange freight, a change that one transportation attorney recently laid out in detail for a room full of freight professionals who sit squarely in its blast radius.
The attorney, Matthew Leffler , an adjunct law professor at Michigan State University College of Law who goes by The Armchair Attorney and has practiced for 16 years, was blunt about the stakes. Fielding live questions at a town-hall session of the FreightWaves Freight Brokerage Compliance Symposium, he ranged across broker liability after Montgomery, nuclear verdicts, FMCSA enforcement, carrier vetting, drop-trailer strategy, and the newer category of AI-driven risk, but the thread tying all of it together was one warning. He argued that what is happening right now on the liability front is as profound a shift for freight as deregulation was in the late 1970s, maybe as profound as containerization , and that ten years from now the business will look almost unrecognizable because of the legal pressure building on it. None of what follows is legal advice, and Leffler said as much repeatedly, but the picture he painted and the practical guidance he offered are worth every broker and every small carrier understanding in detail.
The Case That Changes The Math
The facts, as Leffler described them, are ordinary right up until they are catastrophic. A broker worked with a shipper, sourced a carrier called Lupus Superior, and the carrier moved the load. That carrier held a satisfactory safety rating, which is rarer than most people think, because by Leffler’s count roughly 94 percent of trucking companies carry no safety rating at all, not satisfactory, not conditional, not unsatisfactory. On paper this was about as good a carrier as a broker could ask for.
Then the human element broke the chain. By Leffler’s account of the trial evidence, the driver told his dispatcher he was not feeling well, the dispatcher relayed that to the broker, C.H. Robinson, and the question of whether to swap in another driver came up. For reasons that may never be fully clear, the sick driver took the load anyway. The truck hit stopped traffic on Interstate 20 in Mississippi, and the fire that followed killed three people, seriously injured two more, and killed the driver himself. The lawsuit named the driver, the carrier, and the broker.
Here is where Leffler said brokers need to pay close attention, because two separate strands drove the outcome. The first was ordinary negligence tied to carrier selection, the kind of claim Montgomery made familiar, though the picture here is murkier than a clean selection verdict, since the jury actually answered no to one broker-negligence question and its general negligence finding only left room for a selection theory rather than squarely resting on one. What is not in dispute is the number, because the jury found the broker 23 percent negligent on a 604 million dollar award, which is already staggering. The second strand is the one that should keep brokers up at night, vicarious liability, the old principle of respondeat superior, let the master answer. The plaintiffs argued, and the jury agreed, that the broker had exercised enough control to make the driver effectively its own borrowed employee. Once that happened, the driver’s own negligence, which the jury put at 45 percent, got stacked onto the broker’s share. That brings the broker to 68 percent. And in Texas, where liability over 50 percent triggers joint-and-several liability, being 68 percent responsible means being on the hook for the entire amount. It is worth being precise about where this stands, because no final judgment has been entered. C.H. Robinson has characterized the July 23 result as an advisory verdict that is still subject to post-trial proceedings, and the company has said it will appeal.
Leffler’s point was that this is not a narrow, one-off result. If the borrowed-employee theory holds up through appeal, the entire premise of brokerage, that you arrange transportation using carriers who are not your employees, is in question, and by extension so is the model behind companies like FedEx Ground, Amazon’s delivery network, Uber, and DoorDash, all of which exert far more control over their drivers than C.H. Robinson ever did here. He expects the case to be litigated for five or six years, all the way to the Texas Supreme Court, with no clean way around it in the meantime.
Why A Tracking App Became A Liability
The detail that turned control from an abstraction into evidence was technology. Leffler explained that C.H. Robinson used a proprietary application to track the load, and the plaintiffs convinced the jury that an app living on the driver’s phone for that shipment looked a lot like control, a lot like the driver was furthering the broker’s business, which supported treating him as a borrowed employee.
Leffler was candid that he personally thinks the distinction should be legally irrelevant, that a tracking app tells you when freight will arrive and does not actually direct how a driver drives. But he was equally clear that what should matter and what a jury believes are two different things, especially when that jury has just watched dashcam video of a person burning to death. His hard-earned takeaways were specific. He said he would never use a proprietary tracking app again, because all a plaintiff attorney has to do is convince a jury that the app the broker built controls the driver, and most jurors do not understand how the technology actually works. He urged using third-party telematics platforms rather than homegrown tools, framing the data as tracking the load rather than the driver. And he stressed that language matters, that a broker should talk about being contracted with a carrier, never about having hired a driver, because word choice becomes exhibit text in a courtroom.
The Wave Is Bigger Than One Case
To show what juries are willing to do, Leffler pointed to the Werner Enterprises case, where a truck traveling under the speed limit in icy conditions was struck by another vehicle that crossed a wide median, and the jury still found Werner 70 percent responsible for a 90 million dollar award even though the Werner driver had done little wrong. The appellate story matters as much as the verdict, though, because the Texas Supreme Court reversed and dismissed that result in June 2025, finding that Werner’s truck was not a legal cause of the crash. The same court went the industry’s way again on May 15, 2026, in the matter involving Home Depot, holding that a shipper that simply hands freight to a federally registered carrier owes no duty to the motoring public and ordering the negligent-selection claims dismissed, a point Leffler has made in his own writing. Read together the pair shows a system pulling in two directions at once, juries willing to assign enormous liability and at least one state’s highest court willing to claw it back, which is exactly the kind of uncertainty that makes planning so hard.
The economics explain why this keeps happening. Leffler described a plaintiff’s bar that treats freight as a gold mine, working on contingency fees around 33 percent, now backed by litigation-funding investors who buy a stake in the eventual recovery, which gives plaintiff attorneys the budget to run a dozen mock trials where a defense firm might manage one. He reminded the room that civil cases turn on preponderance of the evidence, just 51 percent, not the criminal standard of beyond a reasonable doubt, so a jury only has to believe you are slightly more likely wrong than right. Meanwhile the structural backdrop is ugly, with the federal minimum carrier liability insurance still sitting at 750,000 dollars, a number set back in the 1980s, a national out-of-service rate around 22 percent for commercial vehicles, and brokers now moving close to 30 percent of the nation’s freight. Underinsured carriers, deferred maintenance, and a public that has no idea how any of this works add up to an environment where even winning can cost millions and years.
The Survival Playbook
Leffler is not a fatalist, and he closed with concrete guidance that brokers should validate with their own outside counsel and insurers. The centerpiece is a written policy that gets updated regularly and, above all, gets enforced rigidly. His warning was that a great policy you do not follow is worse than no policy at all, because the moment you deviate from it on the load that ends in a fatality, a plaintiff attorney will hold up your own written standard and tell the jury you lied. He was unsentimental about enforcement, saying that if people deviate from the written process you write them up, and if they keep doing it you let them go, because a single person freelancing at 2 a.m. on a Saturday can sink the company.
The rest of his advice followed the same logic of limiting control and controlling information. Route all communication through dispatch and avoid speaking directly to drivers whenever a carrier has a dispatcher, because direct driver contact opens the door to knowledge you do not want, like learning a driver is unwell and then being blamed for letting them roll. Understand that indemnification clauses in shipper contracts only protect you if you are still solvent when the litigation ends, so an indemnity from a bankrupt broker is worthless. Carry real liability coverage beyond the mandatory 75,000 dollar surety bond, including contingent auto and cargo protection, because fighting one of these cases without insurance can run 20,000 to 30,000 dollars a month. And assume that every record in your transportation management system will be discovered and read back to a jury, so the metadata trail needs to match the policy you claim to follow.
Leffler was honest about the bind this creates, that following every rule to the letter can leave a broker at a competitive disadvantage against those who cut corners, and that the pressure to keep a long-trusted carrier or customer moving is real. His answer was that brokers and small carriers are not adversaries in this, they exist because of each other, and the real winners of this liability wave are the large asset-based carriers who have carried this kind of exposure for decades and simply raise their insurance towers and move on. The operators most exposed are the small brokers and small carriers who can least afford a single catastrophic claim.
Why It Matters
A jury’s 604 million dollar finding against a broker over ordinary brokering, with a clean carrier and a routine tracking app and before any final judgment has even been entered, tells every broker and the small carriers they depend on that the old assumption of being insulated from a crash several steps down the chain is gone, and that control, communication, and documentation are now the difference between surviving a claim and being bankrupted by one. The practical response is not to panic but to build and rigidly enforce a written compliance process, rethink proprietary tracking and direct driver contact, and carry enough real insurance to still be standing when the litigation ends, because in this environment the goal is not only to do everything right but to be able to prove it years later in front of a jury that does not care how freight moves.
This article is based on a town-hall session with attorney Matthew Leffler, an adjunct professor at Michigan State University College of Law known as The Armchair Attorney, at the FreightWaves Freight Brokerage Compliance Symposium. Case details, figures, and guidance are as presented by the speaker and reflect his analysis, not legal advice. The C.H. Robinson result is an advisory verdict subject to post-trial proceedings and appeal, with no final judgment entered. The Werner and Home Depot verdicts referenced were later reversed by the Texas Supreme Court.

Posted By: FREDERIC TOMESCO October 27, 2026
New drilling by Iamgold (TSX: IMG; NYSE: IAG) has extended gold mineralization at its Nelligan complex in Quebec, strengthening a development project that could provide another source of Canadian growth for the Toronto-based producer.
Drill hole NE-26-272 cut 77 metres grading 2.23 grams gold per tonne from 692 metres downhole at Nelligan’s zone 36, Iamgold said Tuesday in a statement . At nearby Monster Lake, hole ML-26-318 returned 7.3 metres at 49.6 grams gold from 32 metres depth.
Iamgold is targeting an updated resource estimate for Nelligan within weeks and an exploration update for the complex in the first half of 2027, followed by a preliminary economic assessment. The company is studying a shared plant for the surrounding deposits, and the complex is its largest exploration spending priority this year.
“Overall, we view the results positively, with the Nelligan intervals and extension at depth at Monster Lake supporting potential resource growth and conversion,” National Bank Financial mining analyst Mohamed Sidibé said in a note.
Central plant
Iamgold envisages a central processing plant supplied by several nearby deposits, combining Nelligan’s large, lower-grade resource with potential higher-grade underground feed from Monster Lake. The properties sit in an established mining region near Chibougamau, about 700 km northwest of Montreal, offering the company a concentrated development opportunity in Quebec.
Nelligan, Monster Lake and Philibert are located within a 15 km radius, “supporting Iamgold’s conceptual vision of a district-scale operation,” TD Securities mining analyst Steve Green said Tuesday in a note.
Iamgold has expanded Nelligan’s 2026 drilling plan to 30,000 metres from 18,000 metres, mostly to improve resource confidence.
Iamgold has budgeted about $24 million (C$33.6 million), or almost half its planned 2026 exploration spending, for the Nelligan complex. The property could eventually complement Côté Gold in Ontario and Westwood in Quebec, alongside Essakane in Burkina Faso. Those operating mines support the company’s 2026 attributable production guidance of 720,000 to 820,000 ounces.
Nelligan “represents Iamgold’s next major organic growth lever beyond Côté-Gosselin ,” RBC Capital Markets mining analyst Harrison Reynolds said in a note.
Regional strategy
Nelligan hosts 122 million indicated tonnes grading 0.95 gram gold for contained metal of 3.7 million oz. gold, plus 151 million inferred tonnes at 0.96 gram gold for about 4.6 million ounces. Those year-end 2025 resources give the project substantial scale, although the lower-confidence inferred material requires more drilling before it can support conversion to reserves.
At Philibert, the third deposit covered by Tuesday’s update, drill hole PB-26-581 in the Arctic Fox depth extension intersected 29.3 metres grading 3.39 grams gold from 468.1 metres depth. Drilling also extended Monster Lake’s Megane zone to 600 metres vertical depth.
Iamgold’s regional strategy has taken shape through successive acquisitions. The company secured full ownership of Nelligan by completing its purchase of partner Vanstar in February 2024. It then acquired Northern Superior and Orbec in December 2025, bringing Philibert, Chevrier and additional exploration ground into the portfolio.
Consolidating those properties allows the company to assess development across the district rather than treating each deposit separately.
Iamgold shares rose 1.1% to C$23.17 on Tuesday morning in Toronto, valuing the company at about C$13.1 billion. The stock has traded between C$13.30 and C$34.09 in the past year.
